vignette: The rain begins just before he boards the rear car. He is twenty-nine, running his third year as a conductor on the regional rail line. The system hums around him, familiar and predictable, until 6:14 p.m. At the Mercer Street crossing, the signal malfunctions. He watches a sedan slow at the red light, hesitates, then pushes forward. He sees the driver’s eyes widen, sees the hands lock on the wheel. The train moves at forty miles per hour. The impact echoes through the floorboards, a heavy, splintering report that travels straight up Elias’s spine. He kills the power, runs forward through the connecting doors, and steps onto the platform. A young woman lies in the gravel, her coat twisted around her legs, her breath shallow and fast. He calls for help, his voice steady despite the vibration in his hands. He stays with her until the medics arrive, watching the stretcher lift her off the ground, watching her scarf catch on the edge of the rail. He boards the train. The doors close. He tells himself he needs to focus. In the days that follow, the rhythm of the tracks feels different. The familiar click of the wheels becomes a countdown. He starts checking his watch at every stop, counting the seconds between his heartbeat and the sound of the city. He stops answering his phone after midnight. When he sleeps, he dreams of the gap between the train and the crossing, the exact distance the car traveled after the hesitation. He wakes at 3 a.m., heart hammering, pressing his palms flat against his thighs until the shaking stops. He tells himself it’s just exhaustion. He means it, in the way men mean it when they have already rehearsed the words. Weeks stretch into months. He begins taking the long route to the depot, avoiding the Mercer Street crossing even though it adds twenty minutes to his commute. Passengers notice the change. The regular commuters see him scan the platform twice before stepping forward, count the gap between the car and the edge, keep his shoulders rigid. He answers their questions with short nods and polite smiles. He goes to the mosque on Fridays because his uncle asks, because the rhythm of the prayers gives his mind a place to rest. He doesn’t pray like he used to. His thoughts keep returning to the driver’s face, to the split second of dawning fear, to the question that loops in his head: what if he had blown the horn sooner? What if he had braked three seconds earlier? He knows, logically, that the train’s momentum made it impossible. His body doesn’t believe him. Now, at twenty-nine, he clocks out at 6:40 p.m. and walks to the bus stop, keeping his back to the tracks. He counts his steps like a metronome. The city hums around him, indifferent and alive. He unlocks his apartment, hangs his coat on the same hook, pours a glass of water. He sits on the edge of his bed, listening to the distant sound of a train passing through the neighborhood. He doesn’t flinch. He just watches the window, waiting for the vibration in the floor to fade.
